imo-1971-01.title: Pair the terms after sorting; explicit counterexamples
imo-1971-01.body:
Write $S=\sum_{i=1}^nT_i$ with $T_i=\prod_{j\ne i}(a_i-a_j)$. $S$ is symmetric in the $a_i$, so for $n=3,5$ we may assume $a_1\ge a_2\ge\dots\ge a_n$.

**$n=3$.** $T_1+T_2=(a_1-a_2)\big[(a_1-a_3)-(a_2-a_3)\big]=(a_1-a_2)^2\ge0$, and $T_3=(a_1-a_3)(a_2-a_3)\ge0$. So $S\ge0$.

**$n=5$.**
- $T_1+T_2=(a_1-a_2)\big[(a_1-a_3)(a_1-a_4)(a_1-a_5)-(a_2-a_3)(a_2-a_4)(a_2-a_5)\big]\ge0$, because $a_1-a_2\ge0$ and $a_1-a_j\ge a_2-a_j\ge0$ for $j=3,4,5$.
- $T_3=(a_3-a_1)(a_3-a_2)\cdot(a_3-a_4)(a_3-a_5)$ is a product of two non-negative numbers ($(-)(-)$ and $(+)(+)$), so $T_3\ge0$.
- $T_4+T_5=(a_4-a_5)\big[(a_1-a_5)(a_2-a_5)(a_3-a_5)-(a_1-a_4)(a_2-a_4)(a_3-a_4)\big]\ge0$, because $a_j-a_5\ge a_j-a_4\ge0$ for $j=1,2,3$. (Here $T_5=(a_1-a_5)(a_2-a_5)(a_3-a_5)(a_4-a_5)$ and $T_4=-(a_1-a_4)(a_2-a_4)(a_3-a_4)(a_4-a_5)$.)

So $S\ge0$.

**Even $n\ge4$.** Take $a_1=0$, $a_2=\dots=a_n=1$. Every $T_i$ with $i\ge2$ contains a factor $1-1=0$, and $T_1=(0-1)^{n-1}=-1$ since $n-1$ is odd. So $S=-1<0$.

**Odd $n\ge7$.** Take $a_1=a_2=a_3=0$, $a_4=1$, $a_5=\dots=a_n=2$ (at least three $2$'s). Then $T_1,T_2,T_3$ contain a factor $0-0$, and $T_5,\dots,T_n$ contain a factor $2-2$, so they vanish, while
$$T_4=(1-0)^3(1-2)^{n-4}=-1$$
because $n-4$ is odd. So $S=-1<0$.

Hence the assertion holds exactly for $n=3$ and $n=5$. ∎

imo-1971-02.title: Volume argument with the doubled polyhedron
imo-1971-02.body:
Let $V>0$ be the volume of $P_1$ and let $P'$ be the image of $P_1$ under the homothety $h$ with centre $A_1$ and ratio $2$, $h(Y)=2Y-A_1$ (points as vectors). Then $\operatorname{vol}(P')=8V$.

**Each $P_i$ lies in $P'$.** A point of $P_i$ has the form $X+A_i-A_1$ with $X\in P_1$. Since $P_1$ is convex and contains $X$ and $A_i$, it contains their midpoint $M=\frac{X+A_i}{2}$, and
$$X+A_i-A_1=2M-A_1=h(M)\in P' .$$

**Conclusion.** Suppose no two of $P_1,\dots,P_9$ had a common interior point, i.e. their interiors were pairwise disjoint. The boundary of a polyhedron has volume zero, so the volumes would add up:
$$9V=\sum_{i=1}^9\operatorname{vol}(P_i)=\operatorname{vol}\Big(\bigcup_i P_i\Big)\le\operatorname{vol}(P')=8V,$$
a contradiction. Hence two of the polyhedra share an interior point. ∎

imo-1971-03.title: Inductive construction with Euler's theorem
imo-1971-03.body:
We construct an infinite sequence $n_1,n_2,\dots$ of pairwise coprime numbers of the form $2^k-3$, all greater than $1$. Start with $n_1=2^3-3=5$.

Suppose $n_1,\dots,n_m>1$ have been chosen and are pairwise coprime; let $s=n_1n_2\cdots n_m$. Each $n_i$ is odd, so $s$ is odd, and $s\ge5$. By Euler's theorem $2^{\varphi(s)}\equiv1\pmod s$. Put
$$n_{m+1}=2^{\varphi(s)}-3\equiv1-3=-2\pmod s .$$
Since $s$ is odd, $\gcd(n_{m+1},s)=\gcd(-2,s)=1$, so $n_{m+1}$ is coprime to every $n_i$.

It is of the required form and greater than $1$: $\varphi(s)$ is even for $s\ge3$ and $\varphi(s)=2$ only for $s\in\{3,4,6\}$, so $\varphi(s)\ge4$ and $n_{m+1}\ge2^4-3=13$. It differs from all earlier $n_i$, because $\gcd(n_{m+1},n_i)=1$ while $n_i>1$.

Continuing forever gives an infinite set of numbers $2^k-3$ any two of which are relatively prime. ∎

imo-1971-04.title: Unfolding the tetrahedron into a strip
imo-1971-04.body:
**The development.** Draw face $ABC$ in the plane as $A_1B_1C_1$; attach a copy $B_1C_1D_1$ of face $BCD$ on the other side of $B_1C_1$, a copy $C_1D_1A_2$ of $CDA$ on the other side of $C_1D_1$, and a copy $D_1A_2B_2$ of $DAB$ on the other side of $D_1A_2$. We get a strip of four triangles with vertices $P_0,\dots,P_5=A_1,B_1,C_1,D_1,A_2,B_2$, triangle $i$ being $P_{i-1}P_iP_{i+1}$. Neighbouring triangles lie on opposite sides of their common edge, so their orientations alternate; say $A_1B_1C_1$ and $C_1D_1A_2$ are counterclockwise, $B_1C_1D_1$ and $D_1A_2B_2$ clockwise.

The edge $AB$ appears twice, as $A_1B_1$ and $A_2B_2$. Let $g$ be the orientation-preserving isometry with $g(A_1)=A_2$, $g(B_1)=B_2$; for a point $X$ of $AB$ its two copies are $X_1\in A_1B_1$ and $X_2=g(X_1)$.

A path $XYZTX$ unfolds to the polygonal line $X_1Y_1Z_1T_1X_2$ ($Y_1\in B_1C_1$, $Z_1\in C_1D_1$, $T_1\in D_1A_2$) of the same length, and every such polygonal line with interior points on the five edges folds back to an admissible path.

**The rotation angle of $g$.** Let $d_i$ be the direction angle of $\overrightarrow{P_iP_{i+1}}$ and $\beta_i$ the angle of triangle $i$ at $P_i$, so $\beta_1=\angle ABC$, $\beta_2=\angle BCD$, $\beta_3=\angle CDA$, $\beta_4=\angle DAB$. The direction of $\overrightarrow{P_iP_{i+1}}$ is obtained from that of $\overrightarrow{P_iP_{i-1}}$ (angle $d_{i-1}+\pi$) by turning through $\beta_i$, clockwise for a counterclockwise triangle and counterclockwise for a clockwise one. Hence
$$d_4-d_0\equiv4\pi-\beta_1+\beta_2-\beta_3+\beta_4\equiv-(\angle ABC+\angle CDA-\angle BCD-\angle DAB)\pmod{2\pi}.$$
This is the rotation angle $\varphi$ of $g$. All $\beta_i$ lie in $(0,\frac\pi2)$, so the bracket lies in $(-\pi,\pi)$. Therefore **$g$ is a translation iff $\angle DAB+\angle BCD=\angle CDA+\angle ABC$**.

**A shortest path is straight.** Suppose $XYZTX$ is shortest. Keep $X,Z$ fixed and move $Y$ along $BC$. In the development, $F(Y)=|X_1Y|+|YZ_1|$ is a convex function on the line $B_1C_1$, and $X_1,Z_1$ lie strictly on opposite sides of that line. So $F$ has a unique minimum on the line, at the point where it crosses $X_1Z_1$. A local minimum of a convex function is a global one, so $Y_1$ lies on segment $X_1Z_1$. In the same way $Z_1\in Y_1T_1$ and $T_1\in Z_1X_2$, so $X_1,Y_1,Z_1,T_1,X_2$ lie in this order on a line. Let $w$ be its direction from $X_1$ to $X_2$.

At $X$ use faces $DAB$ and $ABC$: the triangle $g^{-1}(D_1A_2B_2)$ is the copy of $DAB$ attached to $A_1B_1$ on the side opposite $C_1$ (since $g$ preserves orientation). The same argument shows that $g^{-1}(T_1)$, $X_1$, $Y_1$ are collinear with $X_1$ in the middle. The direction from $X_1$ to $g^{-1}(T_1)$ is the image of $-w$ (the direction from $X_2$ to $T_1$) under the rotation by $-\varphi$, and it must equal $-w$. So $\varphi\equiv0$.

**(a)** If $\angle DAB+\angle BCD\ne\angle CDA+\angle ABC$ then $\varphi\not\equiv0$, so by the previous paragraph no path is shortest.

**(b)** Now $g$ is the translation by a vector $v$. Every path has length $|X_1Y_1|+\dots+|T_1X_2|\ge|X_1X_2|=|v|$.

*Computing $v$.* Let $C^*=g(C_1)=C_1+v$; triangle $A_2B_2C^*$ is a counterclockwise copy of $ABC$. Put $a_1=\angle BAC$, $a_2=\angle CAD$, $a_3=\angle DAB$, so $\alpha=a_1+a_2+a_3<\frac{3\pi}{2}$. Using the orientations, the rays from $A_2$ to $C_1,D_1,B_2,C^*$ follow each other counterclockwise with angles $a_2,a_3,a_1$. Take $A_2$ as origin and $A_2C_1$ along the positive $x$-axis: the rays point at angles $0$, $a_2$, $a_2+a_3$, $\alpha$. As $A_2C_1=A_2C^*=AC$,
$$|v|=|C_1C^*|=2AC\sin\frac\alpha2,$$
and $v$ is perpendicular to the bisector direction $u=(\cos\frac\alpha2,\sin\frac\alpha2)$.

*Many straight paths.* Let $h(P)=\overrightarrow{A_2P}\cdot u$. Lines parallel to $v$ are the level lines of $h$, and $h(P+v)=h(P)$. We claim
$$\max\{h(A_1),h(C_1),h(A_2)\}<\min\{h(B_1),h(D_1),h(B_2)\}.\qquad(*)$$
- $h(A_1)=h(A_2)=0$ and $h(C_1)=AC\cos\frac\alpha2$.
- $h(D_1)=AD\cos\big(\frac\alpha2-a_2\big)$ and $h(B_1)=h(B_2)=AB\cos\big(\frac\alpha2-a_1\big)$. Since $\frac\alpha2-a_2=\frac{a_1+a_3-a_2}{2}\in(-\frac\pi4,\frac\pi2)$, $h(D_1)>0$; likewise $h(B_1)>0$.
- $h(D_1)>h(C_1)$: in triangle $A_2C_1D_1\cong ACD$ the angle at $C_1$ is $\gamma=\angle ACD$, so $\overrightarrow{C_1D_1}$ points at angle $\pi-\gamma$ and $h(D_1)-h(C_1)=-CD\cos\big(\gamma+\frac\alpha2\big)$. In a trihedral angle each face angle is less than the sum of the other two, so $a_1+a_3>a_2$ and $\gamma+\frac\alpha2>\gamma+a_2=\pi-\angle ADC>\frac\pi2$. Also $\gamma+\frac\alpha2<\frac\pi2+\frac{3\pi}4<\frac{3\pi}2$. So the cosine is negative.
- $h(B_2)>h(C^*)=h(C_1)$: the same computation reflected in the bisector line $\mathbb Ru$ (which fixes $h$ and swaps the rays at $0$ and $\alpha$), using $\angle ACB+a_1=\pi-\angle ABC>\frac\pi2$ and $a_2+a_3>a_1$.

Take any line $\ell$ parallel to $v$ on which $h$ lies strictly between the two sides of $(*)$. It separates $A_1,C_1,A_2$ from $B_1,D_1,B_2$, so it crosses each of $A_1B_1,B_1C_1,C_1D_1,D_1A_2,A_2B_2$ at an interior point. Each of the four triangles has two of its vertices on one side of $\ell$ and one on the other, so $\ell$ meets it in the segment joining the crossing points on its two edges of this list. Consecutive triangles lie on opposite sides of their common edge, so these four segments follow each other along $\ell$ without overlapping. Together they form one segment from $X_1=\ell\cap A_1B_1$ to $\ell\cap A_2B_2$, and this endpoint is $X_1+v=g(X_1)$ because $\ell\parallel v$. Folding back gives an admissible path of length $|v|$. Different levels of $h$ give different $X$, so there are infinitely many shortest paths, all of length $|v|=2AC\sin\frac\alpha2$. ∎

imo-1971-05.title: Induction by translating a copy
imo-1971-05.body:
We prove by induction on $m$ that there is a finite set $S_m$ in which every point has exactly $m$ points at distance $1$.

**$m=1$:** two points at distance $1$.

**Step $m\to m+1$.** Let $S_m$ be such a set. For a unit vector $u$ let $S_{m+1}=S_m\cup(S_m+u)$. Call $u$ *bad* if
1. $u=P-Q$ for some $P,Q\in S_m$ (then the two copies could overlap), or
2. $|P-(Q+u)|=1$ for some $P\ne Q$ in $S_m$, i.e. $u$ lies on the unit circle centred at $P-Q\ne0$.

Condition 1 excludes finitely many vectors. In condition 2, for each of the finitely many pairs $P\ne Q$ the unit circle about $P-Q$ meets the unit circle about the origin in at most $2$ points (the circles are distinct). So only finitely many unit vectors are bad, and we can choose a good $u$.

Then $S_m$ and $S_m+u$ are disjoint. Take $P\in S_m$. Inside $S_m$ it has exactly $m$ points at distance $1$. In $S_m+u$ the point $P+u$ is at distance $1$, and no other point $Q+u$ ($Q\ne P$) is, by condition 2. So $P$ has exactly $m+1$ unit-distance neighbours in $S_{m+1}$. The same holds for points of $S_m+u$, by the symmetric argument (translate by $-u$). Hence $S_{m+1}$ works, and it is finite ($2^m$ points). ∎

imo-1971-06.title: Look at the smallest line sum
imo-1971-06.body:
Let $k$ be the smallest of all $2n$ row sums and column sums. Transposing if necessary (this does not change the hypothesis or the total), assume it is the sum of row $1$. Let $\Sigma$ be the sum of all entries.

**Case $k\ge n/2$.** Then $\Sigma$, the sum of the $n$ row sums, is $\ge nk\ge n^2/2$.

**Case $k<n/2$.** Row $1$ has non-negative integer entries with sum $k$, so at most $k$ of them are non-zero: row $1$ has $z\ge n-k$ zero entries. If $a_{1j}=0$, the hypothesis gives (column $j$ sum) $\ge n-k$. Every other column has sum $\ge k$ by minimality. Adding the column sums,
$$\Sigma\ge z(n-k)+(n-z)k=nk+z(n-2k)\ge nk+(n-k)(n-2k),$$
using $n-2k>0$ and $z\ge n-k$. Finally
$$nk+(n-k)(n-2k)=n^2-2nk+2k^2=\frac{n^2+(n-2k)^2}{2}\ge\frac{n^2}{2}.$$

In both cases $\Sigma\ge n^2/2$. ∎
